Keyboard Accessibility Checklist: WCAG 2.2 Test & Fix Guide

2026-06-04 11 min read

Test keyboard navigation, focus order, visible focus, menus, forms, and modal dialogs with this practical WCAG 2.2 checklist.

Why Keyboard Accessibility Is Non-Negotiable

Every interactive feature on your website must work without a mouse or trackpad. People with motor disabilities, repetitive strain injuries, tremors, and blind screen reader users all rely on keyboard navigation—or assistive hardware like switch devices and sip-and-puff controllers that emulate keyboard input.

If a visitor cannot open your navigation menu, close a promotional popup, select a product size, or submit your contact form using only a keyboard, your site creates a complete roadblock.

Core WCAG 2.2 Keyboard Success Criteria

  • 2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A): All functionality is operable through a keyboard interface.
  • 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap (Level A): Keyboard focus can always be moved away from any component using standard keys.
  • 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks (Level A): A mechanism (such as a skip link) is available to bypass repeated header navigation.
  • 2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A): Focusable components receive focus in an order that preserves meaning and operability.
  • 2.4.7 Focus Visible (Level AA): Any keyboard-operable user interface has a mode of operation where the keyboard focus indicator is visible.
  • 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) (WCAG 2.2 Level AA): When a component receives focus, it is not entirely hidden by sticky headers, cookie banners, or chat widgets.

Essential Keyboard Controls to Test

  • Tab: Move forward to the next link, button, or form control.
  • Shift + Tab: Move backward to the previous interactive element.
  • Enter: Activate links and submit buttons.
  • Space: Activate buttons, toggle checkboxes, and scroll.
  • Escape: Close modals, dropdown menus, and tooltips.
  • Arrow keys: Navigate inside radio groups, tablists, menus, and custom sliders.

Complete Keyboard Accessibility Checklist

  1. Skip link works: Pressing Tab once on page load reveals a visible 'Skip to main content' link that moves focus past the header.
  2. Visible focus indicator: Every focused link, button, and input displays a clear, high-contrast outline (never outline: none without a replacement).
  3. Logical Tab order: Focus moves top-to-bottom, left-to-right matching the visual layout.
  4. No hidden focusable elements: Off-screen mobile menus or closed drawers are hidden with display: none or inert so Tab doesn't disappear off-screen.
  5. Modals trap focus cleanly and restore it: Opening a dialog moves focus inside it, keeps Tab inside until closed, and returns focus to the trigger button on Escape.
  6. No sticky-header obstruction: Focused elements are never covered by sticky navbars or floating chat bubbles (use scroll-margin-top).

Practical Code Fixes for Keyboard Accessibility

1. Accessible Focus Styles

:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #0b5fff;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

/* Prevent sticky header from hiding focused targets */
[id] {
  scroll-margin-top: 96px;
}

2. Use Native Buttons Instead of Clickable Divs

<!-- Avoid: not keyboard focusable or operable with Enter/Space -->
<div class="menu-toggle" onclick="toggleMenu()">Menu</div>

<!-- Accessible -->
<button type="button" class="menu-toggle" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="main-nav">Menu</button>

Next Steps

Unplug your mouse for five minutes and try completing your main user journey—from homepage to contact form or checkout. If you hit a dead end, read how to test website accessibility manually or book a manual WCAG accessibility audit.
